title: Quick Images & Splat
subtitle: Flash a visual, hide it, and ask “how much — and how did you see it?” Builds number sense and fraction/decimal reasoning through what the eyes notice.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Steve Wyborney, Splat! & Quick Images · Fosnot & Dolk, Young Mathematicians at Work (visual models) · NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014).

blocks.text: A **Quick Image** is a visual shown for just a few seconds, then hidden. Students figure out *how much* they saw and — the important part — *how* they saw it. Because the image disappears, students can’t count one-by-one; they have to **structure** what they saw.

**Splat!** (Steve Wyborney) is a variation: a total is shown, then part of it is covered by a “splat,” and students reason out the hidden amount. Both routines turn seeing into reasoning — perfect for part–whole thinking with fractions, decimals, and arrays.

blocks.title: Why a visual routine in grades 6–8

blocks.text: Middle-school fraction and decimal trouble is usually a *part–whole* problem: students manipulate symbols they can’t picture. A fraction bar or area model shown briefly forces students to *see* the quantity — and seeing it is the conceptual foundation that fluency grows from.

blocks.label: Strands of Mathematical Proficiency
items: Conceptual understanding
Procedural fluency
Adaptive reasoning

blocks.label: Effective Teaching Practices
items: Use & connect representations
Facilitate meaningful discourse
Pose purposeful questions
**Flash the image** for 3–5 seconds, then hide it. No counting allowed — that’s the point.
**Silent think.** “How much did you see? How did you see it?”
**Flash again** briefly if needed, then hide.
**Share strategies.** “I saw it as…” Different students grouped or chunked the same image differently — record each way.
**Reveal & connect.** Show the image; connect the ways of seeing to the mathematics (e.g., `3/4` seen as “one whole minus a quarter” vs. “three quarters”).
**Fraction bars & area models** — “how much is shaded?”
**Number lines** with a point to locate or a jump to name
**Arrays / dot arrangements** — for multiplication and the distributive idea
**Splat** — a known total, part covered: “how many are under the splat?”
**Decimal grids** (hundredths) — “what part is shaded?”

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: “I saw it as…” with different groupings shared
Students describing structure, not counting by ones
The same image seen multiple valid ways
Connections to symbols at the end (“so that’s 3/4”)

no.title: We should *not* see
items: The image left up so students count one-by-one
Only the final number, no “how you saw it”
One “correct” way of seeing enforced
The teacher narrating instead of students
**Very low language load** — one of the most accessible routines for multilingual learners; the mathematics enters through the eyes, and gestures can carry explanation while language develops.
**Multiple ways of seeing are all valid**, so there are many right answers to contribute — a wide door for students who doubt they’re “good at math.”
**Visual & concrete** supports students with IEPs who benefit from non-symbolic entry points.

blocks.text: Free, ready-made images and Splat decks are widely available (Steve Wyborney shares full sets). Start with images that can be seen 2–3 different ways — that’s what fuels the discussion.

sections.label: Lesson design connection
sections.sources: Sources: Steve Wyborney, Splat! & Quick Images · Fosnot & Dolk, Young Mathematicians at Work · NCTM, Principles to Actions.

blocks.text: An **Opener routine** — reach for it when your purpose is to build the **visual, part–whole foundation** under a fraction, decimal, or multiplication idea.

Choose Quick Images when students are manipulating symbols they can’t yet picture. A 10-minute image routine that has students *see* three-fourths before a lesson on operating with fractions gives them a mental model to reason from minutes later.

blocks.title: The whole game: “how did you see it?”

blocks.text: The answer matters less than the structure. When you consistently ask “how did you see it?” and record several ways, students learn that mathematics is about *reasoning about structure*, not recalling a number — and that there are many valid paths.

items: **Pick the big idea** (e.g., equivalent fractions, decimal place value, “of” as scaling).
**Choose an image that can be seen multiple ways** — that ambiguity is what generates discussion.
**Plan your connect:** decide how you’ll tie the ways-of-seeing to the symbols at the end (the most important moment).
**Optional sequence:** follow with a slightly harder image that nudges the target idea forward (a small “string” of images).

blocks.text: Connecting what they saw to the math

rows: Splat: 10 dots, splat covers some, 6 show

blocks.text: Keep the flash genuinely short (3–5 seconds). If students have time to count, they’ll count — and you lose the structuring that makes the routine valuable. A second quick flash is fine.

items: **Let students gesture** at the revealed image to explain — physical pointing carries meaning while language develops.
**Record every way of seeing** by name; the multiplicity is the access point and the disposition builder.
**Pair a turn-and-talk** with sentence stems (“I saw ___ groups of ___”).

blocks.text: The habit of seeing and connecting representations is exactly the muscle behind **Connecting Representations** in Core Instruction — moving fluidly between pictures, symbols, tables, and graphs. Quick Images builds it in the lowest-stakes way possible.
